directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Asian saber fern wants good drainage in winter and resents soggy, poorly drained soil more than most shade ferns. Stiff, narrow, glossy dark-green fronds arch outward from a central crown, each pinna tipped with a small spiny point and a distinctive backward-curving, saber-like hook that gives the fern its common name. Native to woodlands from the Himalayas through China, it holds its handsome, leathery fronds through winter in milder zones, providing structure and dark color to the shade garden when little else is evergreen. Groom out the previous year's tattered fronds in late winter just before new crosiers unfurl, and mulch new plantings the first winter until well established.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Rochfordianum holly fern tolerates heat, humidity, salt spray, and dry shade better than most ferns, making it a Gulf Coast landscape standard.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Rochfordianum holly fern tolerates heat, humidity, salt spray, and dry shade better than most ferns, making it a Gulf Coast landscape standard. Glossy, leathery, deep-green pinnae are more deeply and irregularly toothed than the straight species, giving each frond a fringed, ruffled outline that reads as more refined and textured in mass plantings. Extremely tough and adaptable, it holds up to coastal wind and salt spray, dry shade under eaves, and heavy summer humidity that would rot more delicate ferns, and it stays evergreen through mild Gulf South winters. Remove damaged fronds after any hard freeze and let new growth flush from the crown; established clumps rarely need division.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Red Beauty colors most intensely with a little morning sun and consistently moist soil.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Red Beauty colors most intensely with a little morning sun and consistently moist soil. Fronds emerge with an unusually heavy wash of wine-red and burgundy across silvery-gray pinnae, carrying more red pigment and less green than most Japanese painted fern selections, an effect that intensifies as fronds mature through the season. Deciduous and easy-going, it dies back cleanly in fall and returns reliably each spring, combining beautifully with green-leaved hostas, heucheras, and other ferns where its unusual color can stand out. Keep soil evenly moist through summer and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Pewter Veil is one of the older, widely proven painted fern selections and adapts readily to average shade-garden conditions.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Pewter Veil is one of the older, widely proven painted fern selections and adapts readily to average shade-garden conditions. Broad, silvery-gray fronds are overlaid with a soft metallic sheen and centered with deep maroon-purple midribs, giving the whole clump a cool, luminous glow that brightens even the darkest corners of a shade garden. One of the earliest painted fern cultivars to reach wide distribution, it received early recognition for garden performance and remains a benchmark against which newer selections are compared, combining reliably with hostas, astilbe, and heuchera. Deciduous and easy, it dies back in fall and simply needs old fronds cut away and soil kept from drying out through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; The King ostrich fern spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the species and needs room to naturalize.

directions: Plant nursery-grown rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; The King ostrich fern spreads by rhizome as vigorously as the species and needs room to naturalize. Selected in the United Kingdom for larger, more robust, upright fronds than typical ostrich fern, this selection forms a bold, vase-shaped shuttlecock of bright green, finely divided fronds that can tower over most other hardy ferns by midsummer, with separate dark, feather-like fertile fronds persisting through winter. It colonizes moist ground along stream banks, pond edges, and low spots by spreading rhizomes, making it best suited to naturalized plantings or spacious shade borders rather than small, contained beds. Where fiddleheads are foraged in early spring, harvest only a portion of each clump's emerging crosiers to keep the planting vigorous.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Japanese beech fern spreads gently by rhizome and self-sows lightly in consistently moist ground.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Japanese beech fern spreads gently by rhizome and self-sows lightly in consistently moist ground. Narrow, tapering, yellow-green fronds are distinguished by a winged rachis — the leaflets connect directly along the stem without gaps, giving the frond a continuous, feathered outline unlike the more segmented look of most ferns. Native to moist woodlands of Japan, Korea, and China, it forms a slowly spreading, semi-evergreen colony that brightens shaded ground with its lighter foliage color, contrasting well with darker-leaved hostas and hellebores. It tolerates average garden soil once established but performs best with reliable summer moisture and a yearly top-dressing of leaf mold.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Ocean's Fury benefits from consistent moisture to maintain its heavily ruffled frond texture.

directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Ocean's Fury benefits from consistent moisture to maintain its heavily ruffled frond texture. A vigorous hybrid selection bred for exceptionally frilled, wavy-edged fronds in silvery-green tones with dark maroon midribs, it brings a bolder, more textured presence than typical Japanese painted ferns while sharing the same easy, deciduous garden habit. The dense, ruffled foliage catches light beautifully and provides strong textural contrast against smoother-leaved hostas, heucheras, and hellebores in a mixed shade planting. Cut back spent fronds in fall or early spring before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep the display full.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, marshy ground, or rain gardens; blister sedge tolerates seasonal flooding and shallow standing water.

directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun at pond edges, marshy ground, or rain gardens; blister sedge tolerates seasonal flooding and shallow standing water. Narrow, arching green leaves form loosely spreading clumps from which upright stems rise in early summer, tipped with distinctive, inflated, papery seed capsules that swell like tiny balloons and give the plant both its common name and a striking textural accent. Widespread in marshes, wet meadows, and pond margins across temperate North America, it spreads gradually by rhizome in consistently saturated soil, making it a useful component of a naturalized wetland or bioswale planting alongside blue flag iris and pickerelweed. It provides cover and seed for marsh birds and requires no maintenance beyond cutting back old growth in late winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade at pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; woolgrass tolerates both standing water and periods of drier soil once established.

directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet to consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade at pond edges, ditches, or rain gardens; woolgrass tolerates both standing water and periods of drier soil once established. Tall, coarse, grass-like clumps send up arching stems topped in late summer by loose, drooping clusters of reddish-brown flower spikelets that mature into soft, woolly, tan-brown seed heads persisting through fall and winter, giving the plant its common name and strong textural presence in a wetland planting. Native to marshes, wet meadows, and pond margins across most of North America, it is an excellent, fast-establishing choice for stabilizing the wet edges of a rain garden or retention pond while providing cover and seed for waterfowl and songbirds. Cut old growth back in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet, saturated to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade at pond margins, bog gardens, or low-water areas; sand spikerush spreads by rhizome to form a dense mat and tolerates periodic drying once established.

directions: Plant divisions or potted plugs in spring in wet, saturated to seasonally flooded soil in full sun to partial shade at pond margins, bog gardens, or low-water areas; sand spikerush spreads by rhizome to form a dense mat and tolerates periodic drying once established. Slender, leafless, rush-like green stems rise in dense tufts from spreading rhizomes, each tipped with a small brown spikelet, forming a fine-textured, grass-like turf across mud flats, pond shallows, and seasonally wet low spots. It is a valuable erosion-control and habitat plant for the shallow-water margins of a constructed pond or wetland, spreading readily to stabilize saturated soil while providing food and cover for waterfowl and shorebirds. Once established it tolerates both standing water and the seasonal drawdown typical of retention ponds and rain gardens.
